metaData.originalTitle: 从 0 开发大模型的 17 种 Agent 架构演进详细拆解
metaData.title: A Detailed Breakdown of the Evolution of 17 Agent Architectures for Building LLMs from Scratch
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically breaks down the evolutionary path of 17 Agent architectures, from single-shot generation to multi-agent collaboration, from the perspective of control flow design, and provides code implementations for each architecture using the agno framework.
metaData.summary: Based on the all-agentic-architectures project, this article reimplements 17 Agent architecture patterns using the agno framework. The author's core argument is that the essence of Agent architecture is not prompt engineering or framework DSLs, but control flow design. The article starts with single-shot generation (Reflection), progressively introducing architectures such as Tool Use, the Observe-Act cycle (ReAct), explicit Planning, verification-driven replanning (PEV), multi-agent collaboration, the Blackboard pattern, and the Meta-Controller. Each architecture is uniformly analyzed through six fixed questions (Problem to Solve, State, Topology, Router, Failure Mode, Upgrade Trigger) and comes with a complete agno code implementation. The article emphasizes that the core of architectural evolution is the gradual addition of control capabilities: state modeling, explicit control flow representation, local error truncation, side effect management, and system termination conditions.
metaData.featuredReason: Tencent's engineering team delivers a structured breakdown of 17 Agent architecture patterns evolved from scratch, covering everything from single-step execution to multi-agent collaboration. Unlike high-level overviews, this piece focuses on engineering trade-offs, making it a practical reference for developers building LLM-powered systems.

mainPoints.point: The essence of Agent architecture is control flow design, not prompt engineering or framework DSLs.
mainPoints.explanation: The author argues that the core of an Agent system lies in state modeling, explicit control flow representation, local error truncation, and side effect management. These are the key factors determining whether a system can be successfully deployed, rather than the quality of model responses.

mainPoints.point: Architectural evolution is a process of gradually adding control capabilities, moving from linear to cyclic to dynamic scheduling.
mainPoints.explanation: From the linear three-step process of Reflection to the Observe-Act cycle of ReAct, and then to the dynamic scheduling based on shared state in Blackboard, each architectural upgrade adds specific control capabilities.

mainPoints.point: The PEV architecture elevates verification to a first-class citizen of control flow, preventing silent error propagation.
mainPoints.explanation: Building on Planning, the PEV architecture introduces an explicit verification step. It performs structured validation on the results of each tool execution, triggering replanning upon failure, ensuring errors are identified and fixed locally.

mainPoints.point: The core of a Multi-Agent architecture is the explicit encoding of cognitive division of labor, not running multiple models in parallel.
mainPoints.explanation: Different cognitive roles (e.g., researcher, analyst, writer) are decomposed into independent Agents, orchestrated through a fixed pipeline or a dynamic scheduler. This enables role isolation, independent debugging, and differentiated tool configuration.

keyQuotes: The essence of Agent architecture is not prompt engineering, nor the DSL of a specific framework, but control flow design.

The so-called 'evolution of agent architecture' is not about pursuing AGI, but about solving an old problem: how to keep a system controllable, explainable, and recoverable in increasingly complex environments.
The essence of PEV is: preventing errors from propagating silently.
The core of Multi-Agent is not 'running multiple models together', but explicitly encoding cognitive division of labor, scheduling strategies, and redundancy mechanisms into the graph structure.
For the first time, the system has objectified 'control flow'.

relatedArticles.title: From Context to Long-Term Memory: Architectural Design and Practice of LLM Memory Engineering
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically elaborates on the necessity of memory engineering for large language models and proposes a hierarchical management, active scheduling, and mind-map organization scheme based on the "Memory Operating System (MemOS)" architecture.

relatedArticles.title: When the Entire Team Goes Zero-Manual Coding: A 10,000-Word AI-Native Development Handbook
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article details the Tencent team's practical experience in transitioning from AI-assisted programming to an AI-native development model, achieving a 'zero-manual coding' development loop through the OpenSpec specification and CodeBuddy toolchain.

relatedArticles.title: Harness Is Not the Goal, Knowledge Is the Moat — Knowledge Accumulation Practices of an AI Engineering Delivery Team
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Based on the engineering delivery practices of an AI Team, this article proposes that knowledge accumulation is more important than workflow orchestration, and systematically introduces a complete methodology encompassing a five-layer knowledge storage architecture, a three-level maturity system, and how workflows serve knowledge accumulation.

relatedArticles.title: From Requirements to Deployment: A Comprehensive Leap in R&D Efficiency with Full AI Automation
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically explains how Tencent's audit team built a fully automated AI delivery platform to achieve end-to-end automation from requirements, design, development, testing to deployment, and shares its evolution path from L2 (human-machine collaboration) to L3 (full automation), along with core challenges, specific practices, and quantified benefits.

relatedArticles.title: Designing a Production-Grade Multi-Agent Harness from Scratch: Architecture, Evaluation, Memory, Cost, and MCP Tool Integration
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically deconstructs the design principles and engineering practices of a production-grade Multi-Agent Harness, covering architecture orchestration, tool governance, state and memory, evaluation systems, cost control, and MCP integration.

relatedArticles.title: One AI Is Not Enough
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: MiniMax introduces Mavis, a multi-agent collaboration system that uses a Leader-Worker-Verifier architecture and adversarial quality gates to solve the pain points of single agents in complex tasks, sharing its design philosophy, technical architecture, cost considerations, and applicable scenarios.

relatedArticles.title: Exploring Claude Code: Understanding Agent Harness | A Conversation with Xinlu Lai
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: An in-depth analysis of the engineering practices behind Agent Harness, using Claude Code's source code as a specimen to explore its three-layer architecture (execution, context, governance) and the ingenious design of memory and context management.

relatedArticles.title: Beyond Cognitive Reconstruction: Stepping into the Engineering Revolution of Agentic Engineering
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a deep dive into the practical journey of Tencent engineers transitioning from Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering, proposing an AI-assisted engineering system centered on context management and tool-oriented design.

relatedArticles.title: You Don't Know Agent: Principles, Architecture and Engineering Practice - Tw93
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically sorts out the core engineering practices of Agent architecture, covering key technical dimensions such as Agent Loop, Harness, context engineering, tool design, memory systems, multi-Agent organization, evaluation and tracing, and demonstrates the implementation of design principles through the OpenClaw open-source implementation.

relatedArticles.title: Harness Engineering: Can AI Write Code in Truly "Mission-Critical" Backend Systems?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article shares the complete methodology—Harness Engineering—practiced by Tencent's CDN LEGO team for AI coding in ultra-large-scale, high-reliability backend systems. Through a five-layer architecture, three key levers (context, constraints, feedback), and multi-model adversarial code review, they built an engineering system that enables AI to safely and controllably produce high-quality code.
